issues.locator: Published §3.3 p.621; same formula in arXiv v2
issues.printed: disc(q)+disc(g)=disc(f)
issues.correction: For local different/discriminant exponents at algebraically closed residue points, use disc(f)=disc(q)+e(q)disc(g), hence μf−aG(1)=e(q)disc(g). The consequence when g is étale is unchanged.
issues.reason: In characteristic 5 take q:x↦u=x² with G=C2, g:u↦t=u³, f:x↦t=x6. The local different exponents are 1,2,5, and aG(1)=1. Thus 1+2≠5 and μf−aG(1)=4≠2, while 1+2·2=5. All maps are separable and f is smooth off 0. The different tower formula multiplies the pulled-back lower different by e(q).

issues.locator: Published Theorem 1.6 proof p.613, fixed-scheme base-change chain; page image checked
issues.printed: (Xi)^σ≅(Xi)^σ×Si{si}
issues.correction: Remove the identification with the closed fiber. Preserve length by étale/strict-henselian base change of the finite-length local fixed algebra with unchanged residue field.
issues.reason: Over algebraically closed k of characteristic 2, X=Spec k[t,z]/(z²+t²z−t), σ(z)=z+t² and σ(t)=t. The map to A¹t is finite flat, X is smooth because ∂F/∂t=1, f is étale off t=0 since ∂F/∂z=t², and σ is an involution. The fixed scheme is k[t,z]/(t²,z²−t)≅k[z]/z4, length 4, supported at the origin. Its closed fiber is k[z]/z², length 2. Thus set-theoretic support at the point does not justify the displayed isomorphism. The needed length-invariance statement survives the proposed henselian repair.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 2.7, arXiv v1 p. 5
issues.printed: "consider the cover π: C̃ → C_{r²a^{ℓ−1}b²} given on the affine patch where z = 1 by π(x, y) = (axy^{−1}, a^{(ℓ−1)/2}(y^{−ℓ} − rb))"
issues.reason: On C̃: ax^ℓ + 2rby^ℓ = 1, with X = axy^{−1} and Y = a^{(ℓ−1)/2}(y^{−ℓ} − rb), one gets Y² − X^ℓ − r²a^{ℓ−1}b² = a^{ℓ−1}(y^{−ℓ} − 1)(y^{−ℓ} − 2rb) (symbolic check for ℓ = 3, 5, 7). This vanishes only where y^ℓ = 1 or 2rby^ℓ = 1, so the map does not land in the curve. With X = axy^{−2}, the difference is identically 0. The point P = π(1, 1) = (a, a^{(ℓ−1)/2}(1 − rb)), which is all the proof uses, is the same for both formulas and lies on the curve because a = 1 − 2rb.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 2.5, case 𝔪 ≠ 1, p. 1137 (published version); the same text in arXiv v1 p. 7
issues.printed: "We need only check that the equation t_1x² + 2rγ^{nℓ}t_2y² = t_3z² has a solution modulo 𝔪 for some choice of units t_1, t_2, t_3 modulo 𝔪. Since we are free to assume t_1 = t_3, there is no local obstruction at 2-adic primes 𝔭 | 𝔪."
issues.correction: With t_1 = t_3 there can be an obstruction at a 2-adic 𝔭 | 𝔪, whenever v_𝔭(2rγ^{nℓ}) < v_𝔭(𝔪). The conclusion still holds. Repair: replace r by rδ^ℓ, where δ ∈ 𝒪_F is divisible by 𝔭^{v_𝔭(𝔪)} for each 2-adic 𝔭 | 𝔪 and by no other prime (it exists because the class group is finite). Then C_{q^ℓr²δ^{2ℓ}} ≅ C_{q^ℓr²} (§2: C_n ≅ C_{nλ^{2ℓ}}), so Lemma 2.3 and the sets S′, S, Σ are unchanged. The clause r ∉ 𝔭 still holds at the odd ramified primes, where the smooth-conic argument uses it. Now β = 2rδ^ℓγ^{nℓ} ≡ 0 modulo the 2-adic part of 𝔪, so x = y = z = 1 solves the congruence there with t_1 = t_3. Alternatively, keep r and choose t_1 ≠ t_3.
issues.reason: Take F_0 = ℚ, K_0 = ℚ(i) and ℓ = 3, which does not divide Disc = −4. §4 replaces these by F = ℚ(ζ_3) and K = F(i) = ℚ(ζ_12), and K/F is unramified above 3. The prime (2) is inert in F/ℚ, so F_(2) = ℚ_4 is unramified over ℚ_2 with residue field 𝔽_4. F_(2)(i)/F_(2) has conductor exponent 2, so 𝔪 = (4). Since (2) ramifies in K, (2) ∉ S and γ ∉ (2); and r ∉ (2) by Lemma 2.3. Hence v_2(β) = 1. Suppose t x² + βt_2y² ≡ t z² (mod 4) with x, y, z units. Then (z/x)² ≡ 1 + βt_2y²/(tx²) (mod 4), which is ≡ 1 mod 2 but ≢ 1 mod 4. But a unit w with w² ≡ 1 (mod 2) has w ≡ 1 (mod 2), since squaring is bijective on 𝔽_4, and then w² ≡ 1 (mod 4). This is a contradiction. An exhaustive search over the 12 units of ℤ[ζ_3]/4 confirms it. Inertness of a principal prime (p) in K is detected by χ(p) = (−1)^{(N(p)−1)/2}, where N is the norm to ℚ; this is the Hilbert symbol (p, −1) at (2), trivial on global units. For every unit value of β/2 there is no solution with t_1 = t_3 and χ(t_1) = χ(t_2) = −1. Yet admissible residues exist with t_1 ≠ t_3: for β ≡ 2, u_1 = u_2 = 1 + 2ζ_3 and u_3 = u_1 + βu_2 ≡ 3 + 2ζ_3 (mod 4), with norms 3, 3, 7 ≡ 3 (mod 4).

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 3.1 (sketch), p. 1136 (published version); arXiv v1 p. 6
issues.printed: "The finite part of the singular series is (ignoring small primes) ∏_𝔭 lim_{n→∞} Nm(𝔭)(Nm(𝔭) − 1)^{−3} #{(p_1, p_2) : p_1, p_2, p_1 + βp_2 ∈ (𝒪_F/𝔭^n)^×}"
issues.correction: ∏_𝔭 lim_{n→∞} Nm(𝔭)^{3−2n}(Nm(𝔭) − 1)^{−3} #{(p_1, p_2) ∈ (𝒪_F/𝔭^n)² : p_1, p_2, p_1 + βp_2 ∈ (𝒪_F/𝔭^n)^×}: the count needs the normalization Nm(𝔭^{n−1})^{−2}. For 𝔭 ∤ β the local factor is Nm𝔭(Nm𝔭 − 2)/(Nm𝔭 − 1)² = 1 − (Nm𝔭 − 1)^{−2}.
issues.reason: The condition is a condition modulo 𝔭, so the set counted has Nm(𝔭)^{2(n−1)} times as many elements as its reduction mod 𝔭. For 𝔭 ∤ β with q = Nm𝔭, the reduction has (q − 1)(q − 2) elements. The printed n-th term is therefore q^{2n−1}(q − 2)/(q − 1)², which tends to infinity for every 𝔭 with q ≥ 3, so the product as printed diverges. With the normalization the factors are 1 − (q − 1)^{−2} and the product converges.

issues.locator: End of the proof of Proposition 2.5, p. 1137 (published version), with the statement of Proposition 3.1, p. 1135; arXiv v1 pp. 5–7
issues.printed: "For each of the infinitely many triples (p_1, p_2, p_3) produced by the above construction, the ideal 𝔱_{p_1,p_2,p_3} := (p_1^{(ℓ−1)/2} p_2 p_3^{(ℓ−1)/2}) is such that any large enough prime factor occurs with multiplicity strictly smaller than ℓ. Moreover the collection of such ideals has infinite support, else we would be producing infinitely many solutions to an 𝒮-unit equation for a finite set 𝒮 of primes, contradicting the theorem of Siegel and Mahler."
issues.correction: The argument needs infinitely many pairwise non-proportional triples. Proposition 3.1 should say so; its proof gives it, since the circle-method count (or Kai's asymptotic) of triples of height ≤ N is ≫ N^{2d}/(log N)^3 with d = [F : ℚ], against O(N^d) triples proportional to a fixed one. The multiplicity claim should be stated for non-proportional triples.
issues.reason: Suppose ε_1 + βε_2 = ε_3 has a solution in units ε_i ∈ 𝒪_F^×. Then for every I-prime π satisfying the congruences, (ε_1π, ε_2π, ε_3π) is a triple as in Proposition 3.1. For it 𝔱 = (π)^ℓ, up to a power of I, so its large prime factor has multiplicity exactly ℓ, contrary to the first sentence. It also yields the same (a, b) = (ε_1/ε_3, γ^{nℓ}ε_2/ε_3) for every π. Proposition 3.1 as stated ('infinitely many triples (p_1, p_2, p_3) (mod 𝒪_F^×)') does not exclude that all but finitely many of its triples are of this form. The paper does not check whether such unit solutions exist for the chosen β. So the step from Proposition 3.1 to the infinitude of X is incomplete as written, though it is repaired by the count in its proof.

issues.locator: Published §2.2.4, second paragraph, p.13, DOI 10.1007/s10240-017-0096-x; also arXiv:1609.00320v1 §2.2.4, p.12. Both parsed passages compared on 22 September 2026; main-PDF screenshot retrieval failed.
issues.printed: une K-algèbre A admet au plus une norme spectrale pour laquelle elle est complète
issues.correction: Retain a specified topology, or assume the identity between the two complete normed algebras is continuous in one direction. Then open mapping and the valid fixed-topology uniqueness argument apply. The maximum of two complete norms on the same algebra need not be complete.
issues.reason: Let C=C_p, F=Q_p-bar⊂C. Choose t in C outside F, extend t to a transcendence basis of C/F, and extend the automorphism t↦pt of its rational function field to σ∈Aut(C/F). Set ρ_1(x)=|x| and ρ_2(x)=|σ(x)|. Both are complete multiplicative Q_p-algebra norms, but ρ_2(t)=|p|ρ_1(t)≠ρ_1(t). Choose a_n∈F converging to t for ρ_1. Since σ fixes F, this sequence is Cauchy for max(ρ_1,ρ_2), while its individual limits are t and σ^(-1)(t)=p^(-1)t. Thus the maximum is not complete. The report gives all steps and the auxiliary field-theory inputs. This refutes the isolated stronger assertion and its proof step, not the main ramified theorem; an audit of all downstream uses remains open.

issues.printed: p^{i}x_{i,0}=p^{i}fx_{i,1}=\ldots = f^{i}x_{i,i}\neq 0

issues.reason: The relations imposed are p x_{i,j} = f x_{i,j+1}. Substituting once gives p^i x_{i,0} = p^{i−1}(p x_{i,0}) = p^{i−1} f x_{i,1}, and each further substitution trades one p for one f, so that the chain is p^i x_{i,0} = p^{i−1}f x_{i,1} = p^{i−2}f^2 x_{i,2} = … = f^i x_{i,i}: the total degree in p and f is i throughout. As printed, the second term has degree i+1 and is in fact equal to f^{i+1}x_{i,i+1} = 0, since x_{i,i+1} = 0, which would contradict the assertion that the chain is non-zero. The next sentence, p^{i+1}x_{i,0} = f^i p x_{i,i} = 0, is correct.

issues.locator: the proof of Proposition 5.3.5 (published: Proposition 5.23), the step asserting topological nilpotence of the divided Frobenius; present in arXiv v4 and in the published version, and corrected by the 2025 erratum
issues.printed: We claim that the divided Frobenius is topologically nilpotent on its kernel. It suffices to show the same for the surjection A_crys(R) → W(R) coming from the PD-thickening W(R) → R. We recall that A_crys(R) is obtained from W(R^♭) by passing to the PD-envelope for the ideal ker(W(R^♭) → R). This kernel is (topologically) generated by the elements V^m([x]) for m ≥ 0 and x ∈ I := ker(R^♭ → R).
issues.correction: The claim is false. The erratum states: 'The key step in the proof of Proposition 5.23 is to show that for a quasiregular semiperfect ring R, the divided Frobenius φ_1 acts topologically nilpotently on the kernel of the map A_crys(R) → W(R). This is not true.' The counterexample, due to Andrew Senger, is R = F_p[x^{1/p^∞}]/x with the element Σ_{k ∈ Z} p^k [x^{1/p^k}] of A_crys(R), which is fixed by the divided Frobenius and lies in the kernel of A_crys(R) → W(R). The erratum diagnoses the gap: 'While the generators of the kernel of A_crys(R) → W(R) used in the proof do topologically generate the kernel in the p-adic topology of A_crys(R), they fail to do so in the p-adic topology of the kernel itself.' The statement of Proposition 5.23 is unaffected: it was already known by the different proofs of Lau, Displays and formal p-divisible groups, and of Zink, The display of a formal p-divisible group, both cited immediately before it, and the erratum records that 'the arguments of this fallacious proof are not used anywhere else in the paper, so this mistake does not affect any of the results stated in the paper'.
issues.reason: Verified against the erratum itself, which was published for exactly this proposition; the mistake was pointed out to the authors by Akhil Mathew and Andrew Senger. Note that the paper proves a similar topological-nilpotence statement twice more, in Lemma 4.88 (arXiv Lemma 4.9.3) for the kernel of Δ_S → Δ_{S̃} and in Lemma 5.15 (arXiv Lemma 5.2.8) for the Breuil–Kisin prism; neither is retracted, and the erratum's sentence that the fallacious argument is used nowhere else applies to them.

issues.locator: Example 7.3, the two stated ranges in the computation of the cyclic homology of k over W(k); in arXiv v2, the version read (the published version could not be consulted)
issues.printed: Using the filtrations of [antieauperiodic], we conclude for i ≤ 2p−1, π_i HC(k/W(k)) ≅ W(k)/p^{s+1} if i = 2s ≥ 0, 0 otherwise. … Thus, in the range 0 ≤ i ≤ 2p−2, we deduce that π_i HC((W(k),(p)/W(k)) ≅ p^{s+1}W(k) if i = 2s, 0 if i is odd.
issues.correction: The two ranges should be i ≤ 2p−4 and 0 ≤ i ≤ 2p−4 (equivalently i ≤ 2p−3, since the odd groups vanish).
issues.reason: Both formulas are read off from the sentence immediately before them, that LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥s} ≅ W(k)/p^s for s ≤ p−1, applied with s+1 in place of s: π_{2s}HC(k/W(k)) = LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥s+1}. That needs s+1 ≤ p−1, i.e. i = 2s ≤ 2p−4. At the first excluded value, i = 2p−2 and s = p−1, the formula would give W(k)/p^p, but LΩ_k here is the p-completed divided power envelope of (p) ⊆ W(k) — that is, W(k) itself — and its Hodge filtration is the divided power filtration, whose p-th step is generated by γ_p(p) = p^p/p!, of p-adic valuation p − 1 since v_p(p!) = 1. So LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥p} = W(k)/p^{p−1} and π_{2p−2}HC(k/W(k)) ≅ W(k)/p^{p−1}, not W(k)/p^p; correspondingly the relative group is p^{p−1}W(k), not p^pW(k). The conclusion of the example is unaffected: it is drawn in the range 1 ≤ i ≤ 2p−5, where the odd degrees used are i = 2s+1 ≤ 2p−5, so s ≤ p−3 and s+1 ≤ p−2, well inside the range where the de Rham formula holds.

issues.locator: Theorem 4.1, p.13 of the author copy (= arXiv 1810.04801v2, p.13); the JAMS typeset version was not collated (publisher PDF not obtainable here, verification gap G1)
issues.printed: "Theorem 4.1. Let V be a polarized variation of pure Hodge structures of weight k over the punctured polydisk (∆*)^n, with period map Φ: (∆*)^n → S_{Γ,G,M}. Then Φ is R_an,exp-definable." (∆ is the unit disk, p.4.)
issues.correction: Definability holds only after shrinking. For some radius 0 < ρ < 1, the restriction of Φ to (∆*_ρ)^n is R_an,exp-definable, and then for every ρ < 1 by compactness of the remaining annular pieces. The reduction in §4.1 must use charts whose shrunken polydisks still cover the compactification.
issues.reason: Counterexample (n = 1, trivial monodromy). Let f(z) = exp(−(1+z)/(1−z)) on the unit disk, so |f| < 1, and τ = 2i + εf with ε small, so that τ(∆) lies in a disk on which π: H → Γ\H is injective (Γ torsion-free, e.g. Γ(3)). τ is the period map of a polarized weight-one integral VHS. But Φ^{−1}(π(2i + ε/e)) contains the points z_n = 2πin/(2 + 2πin), n ≠ 0, where f = 1/e. These form an infinite discrete set accumulating at 1, which is impossible for a fibre of a definable map. The proof itself allows for this: it says 'after maybe shrinking the polydisk' (p.14), and its Siegel set S_H (y > 1) covers only |q| < e^{−2π}. Theorem 1.3 is unaffected, since §4.1 can use finitely many shrunken charts. Checked numerically: |f(z_n) − 1/e| < 1e−8 for 0 < |n| ≤ 2000. Noted by the extraction (item local-outer-boundary-obstruction).

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 4.5, p.15 of the author copy (= arXiv v2 p.15); the JAMS typeset version was not collated (publisher PDF not obtainable here, verification gap G1)
issues.printed: "Consider for each positive integer m and real number c the function f_{m,c} which we obtain from f by setting z_1 = mz_2 + c. Note that the assumptions of the lemma still apply to f_{m,c}, and it follows by induction on n that f_{m,c} ≪ 1 on all of Σ_{n−1}"
issues.correction: State the lemma, and verify its curve hypothesis, on the wider sectors Σ_n^R = {|x_i| < R, y_1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ y_n > 1} for every R, with constants depending on R. The substitution then maps Σ_{n−1}^{R′} into Σ_n^{mR′+c}, and the induction goes through unchanged. In the application in §4.5, the curve bounds come from Schmid's one-variable Corollary 5.29 and the norm estimates of Theorem 4.8, which hold for real parts in any bounded interval; Theorem 1.5 is already stated on H^n_{R,η} for all R.
issues.reason: Σ_n is defined with 0 < x_i < 1 (Definition 4.4). The proof uses c = 0, 1, …, r_1 and m ≥ 1. For c ≥ 1, x_1 = mx_2 + c > 1, so Σ_n ∩ {z_1 = mz_2 + c} is empty. For c = 0 it is only the strip x_2 < 1/m. So the hypothesis gives no information about f_{m,c} on Σ_{n−1}. The functions extend there (the coefficients in O are periodic in x and f is polynomial in x), but the bound is assumed only on Σ_n. With the R-uniform hypothesis, the finite difference in c isolates the top x_1-degree, the Vandermonde step in m isolates each y-power, and |x_1| < 1 on Σ_n finishes the proof, as printed. Noted by the extraction (verification gap G4); the repair is given by this continuation.

issues.printed: "Then p² strongly divides ∆(f) if and only if f modulo p has at least two distinct multiple roots in F̄_p, or has a root in F_p of multiplicity at least 3; and p² weakly divides ∆(f) if p² | ∆(f) but f modulo p has only one multiple root in F_p and this root is a simple double root."
issues.correction: This holds for odd p. For p = 2, 4 always divides Δ(f) strongly when 2 | Δ(f), so W^{(2)}_m is empty for even m.
issues.reason: By Stickelberger's congruence, the discriminant of a monic integer polynomial is ≡ 0 or 1 mod 4, so 2 | Δ(f + 2g) implies 4 | Δ(f + 2g) for every g. For example f = x² + 1 ≡ (x + 1)² mod 2 has a single simple double root, yet Δ(x² + a_1x + a_2) = a_1² − 4a_2 ≡ 0 mod 4 whenever a_1 is even. issues.printed: "By the uniqueness of Minkowski-reduced bases for these rings, φ must map Minkowski basis elements to Minkowski basis elements, i.e., φ(h_i(θ)) = h*_i(θ*) for all i. An exhaustive search gives the reduced basis 1, ζ_1, ζ_2 with unique minima up to sign. f*(x, y) = f(−x, y) = −x³ − x²y − xy² + y³ has the same lattice R_{f*} = R_f, since ζ*_i = ±ζ_i, so it is strongly Minkowski-reduced too. But f* is not SL_2(Z)-equivalent to f. Otherwise f would have a stabilizer element δ of determinant −1, and −δ would be a nontrivial automorphism of R_f in the twisted GL_2(Z)-action, which is impossible for an order in a non-Galois cubic field. Take x ∈ F ∩ M of multiplicity k ∈ Z_{>0} in M. Then ε_sa(A; x) converges to k when δ → 0."
issues.correction: Only a lower bound holds. For every rational γ with 0 < γ < k there is δ₀ > 0, depending only on f, D and γ, such that ε_sa(A; x) = ε(A; x) ≥ k − γ for all δ < δ₀ and all such A, M, Λ and x. Equivalently, liminf_{δ→0} ε_sa(A; x) ≥ k, uniformly. This is exactly what the printed proof establishes; there is no upper bound.
issues.reason: Counterexample with Λ = 0. Let k be a field of characteristic p > 0, X = A²_k, and f: Y → X the blow-up of the origin with exceptional curve E = F. Let M be the sum of the strict transforms of the two axes. Then M ∼ −2E, so M is effective, Cartier, globally generated over X (O_Y(−E) = m·O_Y) and has no exceptional component. Let x = E ∩ (strict transform of the y-axis), so mult_x M = 1 = k. Blow up x, with exceptional curve G and strict transform E′. Then E′² = −2, G² = −1, E′·G = 1 and π*M − tG ∼ −2E′ − (2+t)G, which has degree 2 − t on E′ and t on G. Hence ε(M; x) = 2. At t = 2 the ideal (x, y²) pulls back to O(−E′ − 2G) (charts x = ab, y = b, then a = c, b = cd, giving c²d, and a = ef, b = f, giving f²). So π*M − 2G ∼ −2E′ − 4G is globally generated and ε_sa(M; x) = 2. Taking A = M and Λ = 0 (any D), ε_sa(A; x) = 2 for every δ, not converging to k = 1. The proof only shows that π*A − (k − γ)E is nef. The consumers need only the lower bound: Proposition 8.15 (p.173) uses the first assertion ε_sa(M; x) ≥ 1, which is correct, and Claim 8.21 (p.178) needs ε_sa > 2 for k = 3. So the paper's results are unaffected. Checked on the page image and by exact arithmetic. issues.locator: Theorem 1.19 of the introduction (= Theorem 7.3), and Remark 7.4(2) (arXiv v4, the version read)
issues.printed: Fix a complete and algebraically closed nonarchimedean field K. Let A be a classical affinoid K-algebra of dimension d. Fix a prime ℓ and let F be an ℓ-power torsion étale sheaf on Spec(A). If A is smooth or if ℓ is not the residue characteristic of K, then H^i(Spec(A)_ét, F) = 0 for i > d.
issues.correction: The disjunct 'if A is smooth' is not proved in the paper at this generality. Theorem 7.3, which Theorem 1.19 is labelled as, proves the vanishing above degree d only for ℓ prime to the residue characteristic; the smooth case is claimed only in Remark 7.4(2), only for constant coefficients, and only as an adaptation: 'The algebraization method used to prove Lemma 7.8 below can be adapted to prove this statement when A is smooth (in the sense of rigid spaces) and F is constant, thanks to [Elkik, Theorem 7 and Remark 2 on page 587].' Either the introduction should restrict the smooth case to constant coefficients and point at Remark 7.4(2), or the adaptation should be written out for arbitrary ℓ-power torsion sheaves.
issues.reason: Theorem 7.3 as printed has two parts: (1) H^i = 0 for i > d + 1 for every torsion sheaf, and (2) H^i = 0 for i > d when F is ℓ-power torsion with ℓ prime to the residue characteristic. Neither mentions smoothness of A, and Remark 7.4 opens 'We would expect that part (2) of Theorem 7.3 holds for arbitrary torsion sheaves', listing the smooth constant-coefficient case as one of two special cases that are 'within reach'. No proof of the smooth case for non-constant ℓ-power torsion sheaves appears in Section 7, and the reduction of Theorem 7.3 to constant coefficients runs through Proposition 7.9 for the two cases actually stated there, not for the smooth case.

issues.locator: Proposition 51 and Theorem 9, Appendix A, pp.36–37 (published version)
issues.printed: "Proposition 51. Suppose L is defined over a number field. Then inf_{φ ∈ Aut(ℙ¹)} ‖a₀(φ*L)‖ = e^{−poly_n(δ_L)}. Proof. … Now the operator L′ := L + 1 is also Fuchsian …"
issues.correction: Assume in addition that L + 1 is Fuchsian. This holds when every finite zero of a₀ has order ≤ n and deg a₀ ≥ n, and in particular for the Legendre Picard–Fuchs operator (87), a₀ = λ(1−λ), n = 2, which is the only operator to which the paper applies Theorem 9. Under this normalization the proof of Proposition 51 is correct, and Theorem 9 follows as written.
issues.reason: For a general Fuchsian operator, L + 1 need not be Fuchsian, and both statements fail. Take L = ∂_t, which is Fuchsian: its only singular point ∞ is regular singular (∂_t = −z(z∂_z), z = 1/t). Then φ(s) = κs gives φ*L = κ^{-1}∂_s and inf_φ ‖a₀(φ*L)‖ = 0. In Theorem 9 take b(t) = (t − t₀)/(2r) (|b| ≤ 1 on D^{1/2}) and f = (t − t₀)²/(4r), so j_z f(t₀) = 0 while |∂_z f(t₀ + r/2)| = r/4, unbounded in r. Here L + 1 = ∂ + 1 has an irregular singularity at ∞. Theorems 1–8 are unaffected.

issues.printed: "At each non-archimedean place v of K, we set η_v := min{1, |t₁(t₁ − 1)|_v, |t₂(t₂ − 1)|_v}. … (µ_{t_i,v}, m_{F,η,v})_v = (µ_{t_i,v}, [F]_v)_v for this choice of η, because the potentials for µ_{t_i,v} are constant on disks of radius η_v."
issues.correction: At places v | 2 take η_v := |2|_v · min{1, |t₁(t₁ − 1)|_v, |t₂(t₂ − 1)|_v}. The claim is then true: in the potentially good range the support of µ_{t,v} is a type II point of diameter |Δ_t|_v^{1/6} = |2|_v^{2/3}|t(t − 1)|_v^{1/3} ≥ |2|_v min{1, |t(t − 1)|_v}, and in the bad-reduction ranges of Proposition 3.5 smaller radii are harmless. (7.5) grows by Σ_{v|2} r_v log 2 = log 2, which is divided by 2|F| and absorbed into C(ε).
issues.reason: The claim fails at v | 2 when |t_i(t_i − 1)|_v = 1. There η_v = 1, but µ_{t_i,v} is a point mass at ζ_{a,R} with R < 1. Indeed λ_{t,v}(0) = λ_{t,v}(ζ_{0,1}) = 0 and f_t(ζ_{0,1}) = ζ_{0,1/|4|}, so the support lies in a residue class of ζ_{0,1} other than that of 0. For x ∈ D(a,R), λ(ζ_{x,1}) − λ(x) = log(1/R) > 0, so the non-archimedean term of Proposition 7.3 is positive, not 0. Counterexample: take ω a primitive cube root of 1 and t₁ ≠ t₂ the roots of t² − (6ω² − 4)t − (3ω − 4) = 0 (discriminant 48ω(1 − ω) ≠ 0). Then ψ₃(ω, t_i) = 0, so x = ω ∈ π(E_{t₁}[3]) ∩ π(E_{t₂}[3]) ⊆ F. Also t₁t₂ = 4 − 3ω and (t₁ − 1)(t₂ − 1) = 15 + 3ω are 2-adic units, so |t_i(t_i − 1)|_v = 1 and η_v = 1. The reduction is supersingular (|j(t_i)|_v ≤ |2|^8), so the 3-torsion reduces to non-identity points and x ∈ D(a_i, R_i). The bound therefore acquires a positive term that is not divided by |F|, which would break the small-height case of Theorem 8.1. With the corrected η_v the equality holds and all later statements stand.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 1.4, p.36 (arXiv v3; published Annals version not collated)
issues.printed: "By the Northcott property and Torelli's Theorem, there are up-to Q̄-isomophism only finitely many C_Q̄'s … such that h(ι([Jac(C_Q̄)])) < c1. By applying Raynaud's result on the Manin–Mumford Conjecture to each one of these finitely many curves separately, we obtain Theorem 1.4."
issues.correction: For each of the finitely many curves C a bound for #((C − P₀) ∩ Jac(C)_tors) uniform in P₀ ∈ C(ℚ̄) is needed, because Theorem 1.4 quantifies over all P₀. For g ≥ 3 it follows from Raynaud's theorem for the surface C − C ⊆ Jac(C): its torsion lies in finitely many points and elliptic torsion cosets, and a coset t + E pulls back to a curve in C × C with no component C × {P₀}, so each P₀ meets it in boundedly many points. For g = 2, C − C = Jac(C), and a uniform Manin–Mumford for the translates C − P₀ is required, e.g. Kühne's later uniform Manin–Mumford theorem (arXiv:2101.10272), which proves Theorem 1.4 without the dependence on d.
issues.reason: Raynaud's theorem gives, for each embedding C − P₀ ⊆ Jac(C), a finite set, with no control of its size as P₀ varies over the infinitely many points of C(ℚ̄). The statement is true, but the displayed step does not prove it.

issues.reason: Take a odd with a² + 4 squarefree, for example a = 13 or 101 (D = 173 or 10205 = 5·13·157). Then D = a² + 4 ≡ 5 (mod 8) is a fundamental discriminant, and a² + 4 is squarefree for a positive proportion of a. For the principal class, (a + √D)/2 has regular continued fraction [a; a, a, …]. A regular partial quotient a in an odd position becomes a run of a − 1 twos in the minus continued fraction, so the reduced period is ((a + 2, 2, …, 2)) with a − 1 twos, and ℓ_A = a. Meanwhile ε_D = ((a + √D)/2)² = (a² + 2 + a√D)/2, so log ε_D ≈ 2 log a, and ℓ_A / log ε_D → ∞. A direct computation for a = 5, 7, 13, 21, 51, 101, 201, 401 gives ℓ_A = a. The 𝒟-module attached to the rank-three canonical zero-p-curvature connection is supported on the zero section, hence on Z'_a; its pushforward has rank 3p and polynomial λ^(3p)=a^p. issues.reason: For Z'=P¹ the stated trace-free Hitchin base is zero, whereas the full homogeneous degree-r section space still contains k·λ^r. It therefore cannot be the claimed vector space. issues.locator: Proposition 21, Proposition 30 and Theorem 3, pp.3, 21, 32–33 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: "Proposition 21. For all unexceptional z ∈ M − K there is a positive constant c⋆ such that as a → ∞, M(z, a) = e^{βa}(c⋆(z) + o(1))" … "Proposition 30. For fixed λ and z⁽⁰⁾ there is a constant c⋆(λz⁽⁰⁾) such that a_L(λz⁽⁰⁾) = … = c⋆(λz⁽⁰⁾) + o(1)" … "Putting Proposition 30 and Lemma 29 together proves Proposition 21"
issues.correction: Add an argument for c⋆ > 0. Fix a small ε₀ > 0 and a point z of the orbit with α(z) > max(C₁, 2C₂^{1/2}ε₀^{−1/2}). Iterating Lemma 26 with ε₀ as in the proof of (3.25) gives log log(λz)_n ≥ log(γ(λ).f(z))_n − 2ε₀ for all λ ∈ Λ′. So M(z, a) ≥ N(f(z), a − 2ε₀) ≥ ½ min_∆ h · e^{β(a−2ε₀)} for large a, since h > 0 is continuous on the compact ∆ (Theorems 13 and 37). Hence c⋆(z) > 0, and then c > 0 in Theorem 3.
issues.reason: Proposition 30 only proves that a_L converges and that its limits are bounded. Neither Lemma 29 nor Proposition 30 bounds c⋆ below. Baragar's estimate (log R)^{β+o(1)} does not exclude c = 0 either, since it allows, say, (log R)^β/log log R. Theorem 3 asserts c > 0, and the constant is Σ over base points of (log z_n⁽⁰⁾)^β c_∞(z⁽⁰⁾), so positivity needs this missing step. The step is routine with the paper's own lemmas.

issues.locator: §9, p. 30 (arXiv v1); checked on the page image
issues.printed: “This looks like a D_3 root system; however, the Weyl-invariant quadratic form in this case is q(s_1, s_2, s_3) = s_1² + s_2² + s_3³ − ¼(s_1 + s_2 + s_3)² rather than the usual dot product, and with this form, we have a realization of the C_3 root system with simple roots α_1 = (0, 1, −1), α_2 = (1, −1, 0), α_3 = (0, 2, 2).”
issues.correction: On the space of characters (s_1, s_2, s_3), where the paper has just written the Weyl action, the invariant form is s_1² + s_2² + s_3² + (s_1 + s_2 + s_3)², and the simple roots are (0, 1, −1), (1, −1, 0), (−1, 1, 1), of type C_3. The printed form, with s_3² for the misprinted s_3³, is the invariant form on the dual space of cocharacters (u_1, u_2, u_3). There the vectors (0, 1, −1), (1, −1, 0), (0, 2, 2) are the images 2α^∨/q(α^∨) of the simple roots, and α_3^∨ = (0, 1, 1).
issues.reason: The paper's reflection for α_3 is r_3(s) = (s_1 + s_2 + s_3, −s_3, −s_2), which is s − ⟨s, α_3^∨⟩α_3 with α_3^∨ = (0, 1, 1) and α_3 = (−1, 1, 1). The computation gives q(r_3 s) − q(s) = (5/4)((s_1 + s_2 + s_3)² − s_1²) ≠ 0, so q is not invariant on characters. A form a|s|² + b(Σs)² is invariant under r_1, r_2, r_3 exactly when a = b. Its inverse matrix I − J/4 gives the printed q on cocharacters. With the roots (0, 1, −1), (1, −1, 0), (−1, 1, 1) and the printed coroots, the Cartan matrix is [[2, −1, 0], [−1, 2, −1], [0, −2, 2]], of type C_3. All this was checked by computation in exact arithmetic. The positive chamber stated next, Re s_1 > Re s_2 > |Re s_3|, is correct, and nothing later uses q.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 6.1, §6.2 (p = 3) and §6.3 (p = 2), p.21 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: "So assume 9|k, in which case (3,0,0) is a non-singular solution modulo 9 and so lifts to solutions modulo 3ⁿ, n ≥ 2." … "So assume k ≡ 1 (mod 4) and we find the non-singular solution (1,0,0) modulo 4 … This then lifts to higher powers of 2."
issues.correction: The two lifts exist only in part of the stated classes: every x ≡ (3,0,0) mod 9 has M(x) ≡ 9 mod 27, and every x ≡ (1,0,0) mod 4 has M(x) ≡ 1 mod 8. Complete the argument with further points. For p = 2 and k ≡ 5 mod 8, use (x₁, 0, 2) with x₁² = k − 4 ≡ 1 mod 8, a 2-adic square. For p = 3, use (3,0,0) when k ≡ 9 mod 27; when k ≡ 18 mod 27, use (3y, 3, 0) with y² = (k − 9)/9 ≡ 1 mod 3; when 27 | k, use (3, 3, x₃) with x₃ a root of x₃² − 9x₃ + 18 − k, whose discriminant 9 + 4k = 9(1 + 4k/9) is a 3-adic square. Each is an exact ℤ_p-point, since the required square roots exist in ℤ₂, resp. ℤ₃.
issues.reason: The gradient of M at (3,0,0) is 6 and at (1,0,0) it is 2, so the lifting needs M(a) ≡ k modulo 27, resp. 8 (Hensel's lemma in the form ‖F(a)‖ < ‖F′(a)‖²). A direct check confirms the two failing classes, k ≡ 18 mod 27 and k ≡ 5 mod 8 (e.g. k = 18, 5). Counting solutions modulo 3⁴ and 2⁶ confirms that Proposition 6.1 itself holds in every admissible class.

issues.printed: "V₃(w) = [[1, 0], [−x₂, −1]] w, so that we write V₁V₃(w) = Aw + b, with A = [[−1 − x₂², −x₂], [−x₂, −1]] … Now, if x₂ ≠ 0, then A has infinite order and Aⁿ − I is invertible … the orbit V₁V₃(p) is infinite if k ≠ 4 … For k = 4, we use instead p = (−1, 2, 0) … and the argument above gives an infinite orbit"
issues.correction: V₃ acts on w = (x₁, x₃) by [[1, 0], [x₂, −1]], so A = [[x₂² − 1, −x₂], [x₂, −1]] with trace x₂² − 2. A has infinite order only for |x₂| ≥ 2, and Aⁿ − I is invertible only for |x₂| ≥ 3, as the paper itself finds for U₂ in §5.2.3. Run the argument with planes x₂ = c, |c| ≥ 3. To show Zariski density for every k, use the points (−t² + k − 4, −t² + t + k − 4, 2) of the parametric family, whose x₂ = −t² + t + k − 4 is unbounded, instead of the single base point (k − 4, k − 4, 2).
issues.reason: x₃ ↦ x₁x₂ − x₃ is linear in w with matrix [[1, 0], [x₂, −1]]. With the correct A the base point p = (k − 4, k − 4, 2) has x₂ = ±1 for k = 5, 3, where A has order 3 and (A² + A + I)b = 0. Its V₁V₃-orbit then has exactly 3 points (checked for k = 3, 5), so the claim "the orbit V₁V₃(p) is infinite if k ≠ 4" fails. For k = 4 and (−1, 2, 0), A is parabolic and Aⁿ − I is singular; the orbit is nevertheless infinite (checked). The density statement for U₁ survives with the repair.

The minimal resolution (charts (x,z,y) = (u,uv,uv²) and (st²,st,s)) is crepant, so K_X is Cartier and m = 1. But div(x) = 2S and the ideal (x, z) is not principal at P, so S is not Cartier. The only other use is Lemma 4.2 (p.16), which needs only that the different of a plt pair with standard coefficients has standard coefficients; that is unaffected. Checked on the page image. issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.1, p.9 (published version)
issues.printed: "Let t_i := Σ_{v|w_i} x_v. Then since |x_{v_{i,j}} − x_{v_{i,j′}}| ≤ 2, we have x_{v_{i,j}} = t_i/k_i + O_k(1). We have Σ_i t_i = 0, since u, α_r, and α_s all have norm 1. Thus Σ_{i,j} max(x_{v_{i,j}}, 0) = Σ_i t_i + O_k(1) = O_k(1)."
issues.correction: Normalise the α_i first. Their relative norms η_i = Nm_{L/K}(α_i) are units of K, since the ideal (α_i) has trivial relative norm. Pigeonhole the α_i by the class of η_i in O_K^*/(O_K^*)^d, which has at most d^{[K:ℚ]} = O_{[L:ℚ]}(1) classes. Within one class, η_i = η₀e_i^d with e_i ∈ O_K^*; replace α_i by α_i/e_i, which leaves the ideal unchanged. Then Nm_{L/K}(uα_r/α_s) = 1, so every t_i = log|Nm_{L/K}(uα_r/α_s)|_{w_i} vanishes, and the stated height bound follows. The loss is a factor O_{[L:ℚ]}(1) in N + 1, so (2.1) is unchanged.
issues.reason: The boxes control only PUL(α_i), i.e. the differences of coordinates within each block, because P drops the block sums t_i. Units u ∈ O* = ker(Nm_{L/K}) have t_i = 0, but an arbitrary generator α_i of ℘_i^{ℓa_i}℘̄_i^{−ℓb_i}℘₀^{−ℓa₀}℘̄₀^{ℓb₀} has t_i(α_i) = log|Nm_{L/K}(α_i)|_{w_i}, the logarithm of a unit of K, which need not be bounded. "Norm 1" in the absolute sense gives only Σ_i t_i = 0. The step Σ max(x_v, 0) = Σ_i t_i + O(1) needs each t_i = O(1) (for example t₁ = T, t₂ = −T gives Σ max ≈ T). So the claimed bound on H(uα_r/α_s) is not justified as written, though the repair costs only a constant depending on [L : ℚ].

issues.printed: "If L, L′ ⊆ V are isometric O_F-lattices of rank n, then we may find g ∈ SO(V)(F) such that L = gL′. We may further lift g to g̃ ∈ GSpin(V)(F) = J(F) such that η(g) = 1. Then the automorphism g̃ of N (see §4.4, 4.5) carries ^𝕃Z(L′) to ^𝕃Z(L). In particular, Int(L) only depends on the isometry class of L."
issues.correction: A lift g̃ ∈ J(F) of g ∈ SO(V)(F) has spinor norm η(g̃) = sn(g) in F^×/(F^×)², so η(g̃) = 1 forces sn(g) = 1. What the argument needs is only val η(g̃) = 0, since g̃ carries RZ^{(ℓ)}_G to RZ^{(ℓ + val η(g̃))}_G (§4.5) and N = RZ^{(0)}_G; that is available exactly when some isometry carrying L′ to L has spinor norm of even valuation, which the remark does not establish.
issues.reason: There are isometric pairs for which every isometry has spinor norm of odd valuation. Take m even and ε = −1: for m even and U unimodular, ϵ(ϖU) = χ(U), so V^−_m ≅ ϖ·H^−_{m,F}. Write H^−_m = M ⊥ ⟨w⟩ with M self-dual of rank n = m − 1, and let L ⊆ V be M with the scaled form, so that all its fundamental invariants are 1 and val(w) = 1. An element of SO(V)(F) stabilizing L preserves L_F and the line L^⊥_F, hence is a product of an even number of reflections in vectors of L or of L^⊥_F (for p odd the orthogonal group of a unimodular lattice is generated by the reflections in its vectors of unit norm, O'Meara 92:4); each such reflection has spinor norm of valuation 1, so the stabilizer has spinor norms of even valuation. Since V is isotropic, sn : SO(V)(F) → F^×/(F^×)² is surjective; choosing h with val sn(h) odd and L′ = hL gives isometric lattices such that every g ∈ SO(V)(F) with gL′ = L has val sn(g) odd. Remark 4.11.5 is the invariance input for Lemma 9.2.2 (i) (the O(W)(F)-invariance of Int^⊥_{L^♭,V}), hence for Proposition 9.2.3 and Theorem 9.3.2. The conclusion is presumably true — Theorem 4.15.1 asserts it, and for m = 4, ε = −1 it follows from Terstiege's explicit formulas (Remark 4.15.2) — and an automorphism of RZ_G outside J(F) shifting the components would supply it; but no such argument is given here, and this extraction did not settle it.

issues.printed: "Let m ∈ M(𝔽̄_p) such that m̂ := ad_M(m) belongs to Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(U)). … Since #F | e, by construction of U[e], we have φ_m(U[e]) = {1}. Equivalently m ∈ Z_M(U[e]). This proves the Lemma with U′ = U[e] and c(N) = e^{k(N)}."
issues.correction: The argument proves the inclusion Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(U)) ⊆ Z_M(U[e])/Z(M). This is what the applications use, and it suffices there. In Lemma 5.11 the Tate hypothesis gives Z_M(V[e]) = Z(M), hence Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(V)) = 1 and so Z_{M^ad}(Û) = 1. Either restate Lemma 5.12 as this inclusion, or supply a separate argument for the equality on U′.
issues.reason: The lemma asserts Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(U′)) = Z_M(U′)/Z(M) for U′ = U[e]. That needs, for every m with ad_M(m) centralising ad_M(U[e]), that m centralises U[e]. The proof takes m centralising the image of the larger group U. Then φ_m is a homomorphism U → F killed by U[e]. For m only centralising ad_M(U[e]), φ_m is a homomorphism U[e] → F, and U[e] need not lie in its kernel, because homomorphisms of U[e] to F need not extend to U. The inclusion needed for the stated equality is therefore not established.

issues.printed: Proposition 5.2: "Let m ∈ Z_{>0} such that Z(m) ≠ ∅; and if b is odd, we further assume that for a fixed D, √(m/D) ∈ Z, as in Theorem 2.4." Lemma 5.3 likewise, with the proof "we conclude by [BK03, Theorem 4.11, (4.73), (4.74)], since both d_0 and k are independent of m." But: "Theorem 5.7. For every m representable by (L, Q) …" and "Theorem 5.8. For every positive integer m, we have the following bounds …", proved from Proposition 5.2.
issues.correction: For b odd and m/D not a square, add this to the proof of Lemma 5.3. In [BK03, Thm. 4.11(ii)] (r odd), the m-dependence through d_0 = d_0(m) enters as log|4m/D_0²| − 2L′(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ)/L(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ). By the functional equation of L(s, χ_{D_0}), this is log m + 2L′(χ_{D_0}, κ − 1/2)/L(χ_{D_0}, κ − 1/2) + O(1): the log|D_0| terms cancel. The logarithmic derivative at κ − 1/2 ≥ 2 is bounded by |ζ′/ζ(2)|, and the χ_{d_0}-factors of σ_m(s) are bounded uniformly as in the proof of Proposition 5.2. So Lemma 5.3 (with O(1) uniform in m) and Proposition 5.2 hold for every m with Z(m) ≠ ∅. That is what Theorems 5.7–5.8 assert, and what Proposition 6.4 and Lemma 7.6 use.
issues.reason:
Theorem 5.8 is proved from equation (3.1), Proposition 3.2 and Proposition 5.2, so for b odd its proof covers only m ∈ D·(Q^×)². It is then applied to arbitrary integers:
- in Proposition 6.4 to M = Q(λ) for a difference λ of two lattice vectors ("Theorem 5.8(i) implies X^{b/2} ≪ −log|Q(λ_x)| ≪ A(M) ≪ M^{b/2} log M");
- in Lemma 7.6 to m = a_1(n)², a square but not in general D times a square.
Both feed Theorem 6.1 and Theorem 7.1, hence the main theorem for every odd b ≥ 3. For b even, d = (−1)^{r/2}det(L) does not depend on m and there is no gap. issues.locator: §7.3, construction of μ, p.43
issues.printed: "We define the a_i as follows: suppose that a_n ≠ 0; we define a_i = 0 for n + 1 ≤ i ≤ e^{e^{p^n}}, and we then define a_i = 1 for i = ⌈e^{e^{p^n}}⌉. This implies that Σ_{i≤n} a_ip^i ≡ μ mod p^N with N ≥ e^{e^{p^n}} – that is, there is an integer x_n of size O(p^n) that approximates μ mod p^N, with N double-exponential in the size of x_n. … the lattice Λ created this way must also have property 2."
issues.correction: Make the gaps double-exponential in the discriminant rather than in x_n: after a_n ≠ 0, set a_i = 0 for n < i < exp(exp(C·p^{2c(n+1)})) with C depending only on L (so that exp(C·p^{2c(n+1)}) exceeds the discriminant of L_n below). Then property (2) of Lemma 7.11 holds with L_n = span_Z{e_j + x_nf_j}, and the example stands.
issues.reason: Property (2) of Lemma 7.11 needs N_i ≥ e^{e^{D_i}}, where D_i is the discriminant of the approximating sublattice L_i. Here L_i = span_Z{e_j + x_nf_j : 1 ≤ j ≤ c}, with e_j, f_j orthogonal and Q positive definite. So D_i ≍ Π_j (Q(e_j) + x_n²Q(f_j)) ≥ x_n^{2c} ≥ p^{2cn}, because a_n ≠ 0 forces x_n ≥ p^n. The printed choice gives only N ≈ e^{e^{p^n}}, which is far below e^{e^{D_i}}, so the proof of Lemma 7.11 (m_i < e^{D_i} and (Y_Λ.Z(m_i)) > N_i ≥ e^{e^{D_i}} > e^{m_i}) does not apply. "Double-exponential in the size of x_n" is not double-exponential in D_i ≍ x_n^{2c}. The example is illustrative and not used for the main results.

issues.correction: For G′ not good, replace lim by liminf: liminf_{q→∞, (q,|G′|)=1} Ẽ^±_{F_q(t),q^{2n}}(G,G′)/|H_2(G′,c)[q−1]| ≥ w_G n^{N_{G′}−1}, and likewise with E^± and a smaller constant in Theorem 1.2.
issues.reason: The proof bounds the ratio from below for each large q. It keeps only the multidegrees n in a set 𝒞 (all n_i large, with prescribed parities) on which the number of Frobenius-fixed components is |H_2(G′,c)[q−1]|, and discards the other components as nonnegative. That gives a lower bound for the liminf. It does not show the limit exists: the discarded components with small n_i and their Frobenius-fixed counts may depend on q, and nothing in the argument controls them. issues.locator: Proposition 14, pp.725–727, and Remark 16, p.727, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 709–744 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 814976ee…f40a); also footnote 4, p.712
issues.printed: Proposition 14: close CM points of the same type with the same projection to X(1)×X(1) lie on a low-degree Hecke curve, stated for Heegner and anti-Heegner CM points alike. Remark 16: "Hecke curves do not pass through anti-Heegner CM points. Thus, …" anti-Heegner CM points repel. Footnote 4: the 2-to-1 ambiguity of [BT13] "can be rectified by using the stronger repulsion statement found in Proposition 14."
issues.correction: Proposition 14 holds for Heegner CM points (CM⁺) only, with Lemma 15 applied with h₀ = 1 (erratum Proposition 2.1). Close anti-Heegner CM points lie on low-degree conjugate Hecke curves instead. The first clause of Remark 16 (Hecke curves contain no anti-Heegner points) is true; its repulsion claim is false.
issues.reason: The real-analytic involution conjugating the second factor preserves the hyperbolic metric and swaps Heegner and anti-Heegner CM points, so anti-Heegner points cannot all repel. In general no h₀ ∈ SL₂(Z) reduces to the non-identity coset of the stabilizer H in its normalizer, which is where the proof fails (erratum §§1–2). The appeal in footnote 4 therefore rests on the withdrawn part; the main theorems hold by the corrected argument of the erratum.

issues.printed: "We say that a curve X is parabolic if it has genus 0 and the degree of X̄ ∖ X is at most 2. If X is proper of genus 0, then there is a unique Galois section, and it is geometric if and only if X = P¹. If X is parabolic affine, every Galois section of X is cuspidal (the only non-trivial case is settled by [Sch15, Theorem A]). Because of this, we can always assume that X is non-parabolic."
issues.correction: The sentence is false as stated. What the later reductions need is a statement about the t-birationally liftable (or birationally liftable) sections of a parabolic affine X, which have to be treated directly, including the case where X̄ ∖ X is a single point of degree 2. The reductions to non-parabolic X rest on this: "We may assume that X is non-parabolic" in the proof of Lemma 16, and "it is immediate to check that t-b.l. sections are quasi-t-b.l." after Definition 18, where the identity map is not available for parabolic X.
issues.reason: Counterexample. Let k = Q and X = P¹_Q ∖ V(T² − 2). Then X is affine, of genus 0, with boundary a single point of degree 2, so it is parabolic. The paper defines a Galois section to be cuspidal if it is associated with a k-rational point of X̄ ∖ X (§1). The boundary has no Q-rational point, so X has no cuspidal sections. But 0 ∈ X(Q), so X has a geometric section. Schmidt's theorem concerns the existence of rational points and splitting; it does not make a degree-2 boundary point rational. The paper's Theorems A–C are not claimed to fail here, only this justification of the reduction. Noted by the extraction (item 77, with the reduction gap in items 81, 96 and 112).

issues.printed: "(ii) The number of supersingular points in X₀(N)(F_{p²}) that correspond to supersingular elliptic curves over F_{p²} with the Frobenius trace a_{p²} = 2p or −2p and the j-invariant different from 0 and 1728 is at least µ(⌊(p−1)/12⌋ − 3/2 + (−3/p) + ½(−1/p)). In particular, there is a supersingular point with a_{p²} = 2p or −2p in X₀(N)(F_{p²}) over X(1)(F_{p²})∖{0,1728} that is unramified for π if p ≡ 1 mod 12 or p ≥ 31."
issues.correction: The "in particular" follows for p ≡ 1 mod 12 and for p ≥ 31 with p ≠ 47. At p = 47 the displayed lower bound is 0 and gives nothing. The existence of an unramified supersingular point at p = 47 comes instead from Lemma 5.2(iii), since 47 ≡ 2 mod 3.
issues.reason: The conclusion needs the lower bound to exceed the number of ramification points, which (i) bounds by µ/6. At p = 47: ⌊46/12⌋ = 3, (−3/47) = −1 (47 ≡ 2 mod 3) and (−1/47) = −1 (47 ≡ 3 mod 4), so the bound is µ(3 − 3/2 − 1 − 1/2) = 0 < µ/6. A computation over all primes 31 ≤ p ≤ 400 finds 47 as the only failure, and beyond that the floor term dominates. The main theorem is unaffected: Lemma 5.2(iii) covers p = 47, and Rubin's own verification (Remark 2.3) covers small p. Found by the review REV-PAPER-BURUNGALE-KOBAYASHI-OTA-21.

issues.locator: Theorem 2.1 and footnote 3, p.4, in arXiv 2506.03465v2 (11 October 2025), the version read; the passage is the same in v1 (4 June 2025)
issues.printed: "Theorem 2.1. Let the notation be as above. Then we have ξ(h²_Q) = ξ((h¹/z)_Q), an equality of ideals in Z_p[[G_{p∞f}]]⊗Q." Footnote 3: "The formulation in Theorem 2.1 is then identical with the one in [11, §7.2]."
issues.correction: ξ((h¹/z)_Q) = ξ(h²_Q)·∏_{𝔩|f, 𝔩∤p} ξ(Z_p[[G_{p∞f}/D_𝔩]]_Q), D_𝔩 the decomposition group of 𝔩; equivalently ξ((h¹/z)_Q) = ξ(H²_Q) with H² = lim_{K'} H²(O_{K'}[1/pf], Z_p(1)), which is the module of Johnson-Leung–Kings §7.2. The printed equality holds when every prime factor of f lies above p, and after localizing at height-one primes on components ramified at every 𝔩|f with 𝔩∤p.
issues.reason: z is generated by the elliptic units of the single modulus p^n f (Kato §15.5), whose projection to a character χ carries ∏_{𝔩|f,𝔩∤p}(1 − χ(𝔩)Frob_𝔩^{−1}) (Johnson-Leung–Kings Lemma 7.7); JLK accordingly pair it with H² over O_K[1/pf]. BT's h² is the class-group limit, which Kato (15.6.2) identifies at height one with H² over O_K[1/p]. By purity, 0 → H²(O[1/p]) → H²(O[1/pf]) → ⊕_{𝔩|f,𝔩∤p} Z_p[[G/D_𝔩]] → 0, and since D_𝔩 has Z_p-rank one each term is torsion but not pseudo-null. On the trivial-character component 1 − Frob_𝔩^{−1} is a non-unit even after inverting p, so the printed equality fails whenever f has a prime factor not above p, and footnote 3's "identical" is false for h². The same imprecision is in Kato's quotation of Rubin (Astérisque 295, Theorem 15.2(2)); Rubin's elliptic units include all moduli g|f.

issues.correction: The count of geometric branches over k-points needs an extra term for the non-rational branches through rational singular points. For a geometrically integral curve C with normalization of genus g and arithmetic genus p_a, one has Σ_{x∈C(k)} #ν^{−1}(x) ≤ #C̃(k) + 2 Σ_x δ_x ≤ q + 1 + 2g q^{1/2} + 2(p_a − g). The constant q + 4q^{1/2} + 3 in Theorem 9.1 and in Theorems 1.5, 1.7, 10.1 and Corollaries 1.11, 1.14, 1.15, obtained from Lemma 3.15 in (9.8), is not established by the v2 argument.
issues.reason: Counterexample. Let D ⊂ P² over k = F_3 be the projective closure of y² = x²(x − 1). It is geometrically integral (r = 1) with normalization P¹, parametrized by x = t² + 1, y = t(t² + 1), so g_g = 0 and the right side is q + 1 = 4. D(F_3) consists of (0,0), (1,0), (2,1), (2,2) and the point at infinity. The origin is an ordinary node with tangent cone y² + x² = 0. Since −1 is not a square in F_3, its two branches t = ±i are defined only over F_9. The left side is therefore 2 + 4 = 6 > 4. The proof's flaw: Lemma 3.17 correctly relates the product of Z*_{D,k}(ζT) over ζ ∈ μ_d to the zeta functions of the C̃_j over k′. But the zeros and poles of Z*_{D,k} cannot be read off from that product. Here Z*_{D,k}(T) = (1 + T)/((1 − T)²(1 − qT)), and the extra factor (1 + T)/(1 − T) disappears under T ↦ −T. The bound with q + 1 + 2g q^{1/2} + 2(p_a − g) follows from Weil's bound for C̃ together with b_x ≤ δ_x + 1 ≤ 2δ_x at singular points, and it is attained in the example. The general reducible, weighted sum in (9.8) needs the analogous count, including intersections of Frobenius-conjugate components. Noted by the extraction (gap G1, items bad-branch-bound and global-sum-source), which checked the page image.

"Log^t_j(y) = Σ_{m≥1} ((−1)^m/m) · Ψ^{[m]}_j(y), Exp^t_j(x) = Σ_{m≥1} (1/m!) · ψ^{[m]}_j(x)", with ψ^{[m]}_j the homogeneous part of degree m of Ψ^{[m]}_j.

The sign: with finite differences, Σ ((−1)^{m−1}/m) Ψ^{[m]} equals the logarithm f, while the printed (−1)^m/m gives −f, which is not inverse to Exp^t as Lemma 7.7(ii) asserts. The bounds used later (|b_{j,α}| ≤ ‖α‖^{[K:Q_p]}, m!c_{j,α} ∈ R) hold for the corrected series, so the main results are unaffected. Checked on the page image. issues.printed: "Proposition 2.2. For a finite, flat map R → R′ of local rings, an open subscheme V ⊂ Spec R, and an affine, smooth R-group scheme G, if (1) Γ(Spec R, O) ≅ Γ(V, O) via pullback; and (2) every G-torsor is trivial over R; then the following pullback is injective: H¹_et(V, G) ↪ H¹_et(V_{R′}, G). (2.2.1)" Proof: "… every element of X(V) lifts to (Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′}))(V), so, by [Gir71, III.3.2.2], the map H¹_et(V, G) → H¹_et(V, Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′})) (2.2.2) is injective."
issues.correction: State Proposition 2.2 for commutative G, which covers both of its uses (Proposition 2.3, with G = Res_{R′/R}(T_{R′})/T, and Corollary 2.4, with G = T). For noncommutative G, supply the missing step: for every G-torsor P over V, the twisted map (^P Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′}))(V) → (^P X)(V) must also be surjective.
issues.reason: Write H = Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′}) and X = H/G. Surjectivity of H(V) → X(V) shows that the fibre of H¹(V, G) → H¹(V, H) over the trivial class is trivial. When G is commutative this is injectivity, because the map is a group homomorphism. For a noncommutative G, H¹ is only a pointed set. The fibre through the class of a torsor P is the orbit set of (^P H)(V) acting on (^P X)(V), for the twists by P (Giraud III.3.2; cf. Serre, Galois Cohomology, I.5.5, Cor. 2). The proof checks only the untwisted case. The twisted forms ^P X live only over V, so hypothesis (1) and the affineness of X give no control of their V-points. If P extends to R it is trivial by (2), so the problem is exactly the torsors on V that do not extend. Proposition 2.2 is used only in the proofs of Proposition 2.3 (G = Res_{R′/R}(T_{R′})/T) and Corollary 2.4 (G = T, an R-torus), where G is commutative, so the main theorems are unaffected. Noted by the extraction (gap G-NONABELIAN, items h1-descent and h1-abelian), which did not claim the statement false; neither is it claimed false here.

Since the discriminant of Zv ⊕ v^⊥ is v² disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X)), this implies by the same argument that |disc(N(X))| ≤ v² |disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))|."

So λ = v²/I² is a positive rational number with λ ≤ v², and I divides v² because v is primitive. For p ∤ v², for example v² = 2 and p ≥ 3 as in the applications, λ is still a p-adic unit, which is what the later arguments use.

For example, in Λ_2d = ⟨2d⟩ ⊕ U with basis h, e, f, take the span of v = e + f and w = kh + e. It is primitive, since (x, y, z) ↦ (z, y − z) retracts it, and its Gram matrix [[2, 1], [1, 2dk²]] is positive definite.
issues.reason: The proof starts from a primitive embedding Λ ⊂ Λ_2d, which the statement does not provide, and the statement fails for non-primitive Λ. issues.correction: No bound ℓ_A ≪ log ε_D holds uniformly. ℓ_A can be about √D while log ε_D is about log D. Eichler's argument bounds the word length of the geometric code of the closed geodesic, which is a different quantity from ℓ_A.
issues.reason: Take a odd with a² + 4 squarefree, for example a = 13 or 101 (D = 173 or 10205 = 5·13·157). Then D = a² + 4 ≡ 5 (mod 8) is a fundamental discriminant, and a² + 4 is squarefree for a positive proportion of a. For the principal class, (a + √D)/2 has regular continued fraction [a; a, a, …]. A regular partial quotient a in an odd position becomes a run of a − 1 twos in the minus continued fraction, so the reduced period is ((a + 2, 2, …, 2)) with a − 1 twos, and ℓ_A = a. Meanwhile ε_D = ((a + √D)/2)² = (a² + 2 + a√D)/2, so log ε_D ≈ 2 log a, and ℓ_A / log ε_D → ∞. A direct computation for a = 5, 7, 13, 21, 51, 101, 201, 401 gives ℓ_A = a. In each case the product of the reduced w over the period equals ε_D, as in (6.3), which confirms that ℓ_A is the paper's quantity. The remark is not used elsewhere in the paper.
issues.known: Partly: P. Humphries and A. C. Nordentoft, "Sparse equidistribution of geometric invariants of real quadratic fields", arXiv 2211.05890v2 (28 August 2025), Remark 3.22, observe that Eichler's argument bounds the geometric code of the geodesic and not ℓ_A (the arithmetic code), so the remark is unsupported. As printed, (6.6) would therefore make the Weyl integrals of u exponentially small in r, which the cited results do not give. For u the two exponentials cancel: Weyl(u, χ) = ‖φ‖ Weyl(⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ, χ) ≪ L(1, sym²φ)^{1/2} r^C |D|^{13/28+ε}, and L(1, sym²φ) ≪ r^ε. A correct witness: for c = a/b with a, b ∈ k[x][[t]], remove the common power of t so that b_0 ≠ 0, and let m = ord_x(b_0). The recursion c_n = (a_n − Σ_{i≥1} b_i c_{n−i})/b_0 gives ord_x(c_n) ≥ −m(n + 1). Every element of Frac(k[x][[t]]) therefore has x-poles growing at most linearly in n, while Σ t^n/x^{n!} has poles of order n!. issues.printed: "Corollary 1.1.15. Let G be an arbitrary connected reductive group over Q_p with a Q_p-rational Levi subgroup M. Let μ: G_m → M be a minuscule cocharacter and [b_M] ∈ B(M)_b such that ([b_M], {μ}) is G-admissible. Then there exists w ∈ W(G, M) := N_G(M)/M such that ([b_M], {w·μ}) is M-admissible." Proof: "(1.1.13) implies that there exists w* ∈ W(G*, M*) such that ([b_{M*}], {w*·μ*}) is M*-admissible."
issues.correction: Replace N_G(M)/M by the absolute Weyl group W(G, T) of a maximal torus T ⊂ M with μ ∈ X_*(T), as in Proposition 1.1.13. Equivalently: some G(Q̄_p)-conjugate μ′ of μ factoring through T makes ([b_M], {μ′}) M-admissible.
issues.reason: The printed statement fails already for split G. Take G = GL_3, M = GL_1 × GL_2 (blocks of sizes 1 and 2), μ = (0,1,0) and b_M = diag(p,1,1), which is basic in M. Then ([b_M], {μ}) is G-admissible: its Newton point (1,0,0) equals the dominant μ̄, and both have κ_G = 1. But κ_M(b_M) = (1,0), while κ_M(μ) = (0,1). Since the blocks have different sizes, N_G(M) = M, so W(G, M) is trivial and no w in it helps. The permutation of the first two coordinates, in W(G, T) = S_3, does. The proof transports to the quasi-split inner form and applies Proposition 1.1.13. That proposition gives w* in the absolute Weyl group W(G*, T*), not in N_{G*}(M*)/M*, so the proof establishes the corrected statement. The only use is in the proof of Corollary 1.1.17, p.13, for G not necessarily quasi-split. It cites "Lemma 1.1.13" (the quasi-split Proposition 1.1.13) in the form w ∈ W(G, T). The corrected Corollary 1.1.15 is exactly what that step needs, so the later results stand. Checked on the page images. Noted by the extraction (source discrepancy 2, items N29 and N32), which also verified the Weyl-group computation by machine.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.2.8, p.28, in the author PDF https://math.berkeley.edu/~swshin/HT.pdf (41 pp., created 27 January 2021, SHA-256 fd22990b…52db), the latest version found; the published text, Duke Math. J. 171 (2022), 1559–1614, was not collated
issues.printed: "Let G′ = G × T, equipped with the symplectic representation V′ = V ⊕ V. Let X′ = X × {h_T}. Then we have (G′, X′) ↪ (G_{V′}, H_{V′}). … Restricting the action of I_{s′_0} to A_T induces a map of Q-groups I_{s′_0} → T, and we consider the composite I_{s′_0} → T → G^ab. By Corollary 2.1.9, I_{s′_0} → I_{s_0} is surjective, so the map I_{s′_0} → G^ab factors through I_{s_0}, as this is true over Q_ℓ for any ℓ ≠ p."
issues.correction: Take G′ = G ×_{G^ab} T, the pairs (g, t) with the same image in G^ab. This lies in GSp(V ⊕ V, ψ ⊕ ψ), and X′ = X × {h_T} still maps into it because h^ab is constant on X. The kernel of G′ → G is T ∩ G^der, which dies in G^ab, so the composite I_{s′_0} → T → G^ab does factor through I_{s_0}. The rest of the proof then goes through.
issues.reason: Read literally, the construction fails at two points. First, G × T acting on V ⊕ V does not preserve ψ ⊕ ψ up to a scalar when the similitude factors of g and t differ, so it is not a subgroup of G_{V′}. Second, the claimed factorization fails. The CM automorphisms (1, t), t ∈ T, act trivially on A_{s_0} and by t on A_T, and they preserve the tensors cutting out G × T. So 1 × T lies in I_{s′_0}, and also in the kernel of I_{s′_0} → I_{s_0}. But under I_{s′_0} → T → G^ab it maps onto G^ab, as T is a maximal torus of G. So the map does not factor through I_{s_0} unless G^ab = 1. The same happens over Q_ℓ, so the justification "as this is true over Q_ℓ" fails too. Surjectivity of I_{s′_0} → I_{s_0} alone cannot give a factorization. What is needed is that the kernel maps trivially, and the fibre product above provides this. Lemma 2.2.8 is used in the proof of Proposition 2.2.2 (p.28). Noted by the extraction (source discrepancy 7, item T23) as a descent gate; the analysis and the fibre-product repair are given here.

issues.printed: "Lemma 2.2.11. Let S be an irreducible scheme of finite type over a field k, and Γ ⊂ S(k) a Zariski dense subset. Let W ⊂ Aut_k S be a finite subgroup, and σ ∈ Aut_k S. Suppose that for every γ ∈ Γ, there exists w ∈ W such that w(γ) = σ(γ). Then σ = w for some w ∈ W."
issues.correction: Assume in addition that S is reduced and separated (for example a variety). Then two automorphisms that agree on a dense set of points agree, because their equalizer is a closed subscheme containing a dense set, and the proof applies.
issues.reason: The proof ends "Γ_{w_0} is dense in S … and it follows that σ = w_0". That step fails without reducedness or separatedness. For the affine line with doubled origin, the automorphism exchanging the two origins fixes the dense set of other k-points; again W is trivial. The lemma is applied on p.30 to a maximal torus T, which is reduced and separated, so nothing changes. Checked on the page image.
